unit.name: Customer support case study: decomposition, workflow mapping, and eval taxonomy
unit.description: Shows how to build and evaluate a customer-support agent by decomposing human work, mapping steps to LLMs/tools/RAG/memory, using traces, and designing objective, subjective, component, end-to-end, quantitative, and qualitative evals.
unit.summary: The case study begins with a product-manager request to build a customer support agent for changing a shipping address [ts=5126s]. The recommended starting point is task decomposition with support agents, identifying what steps are fuzzy, deterministic, slow, or difficult [ts=5195s]. The simplified workflow extracts key information, retrieves a customer record, checks policy, drafts a response email, and sends the email [ts=5236s]. Mapping that workflow requires deciding which steps need a vanilla LLM, a tool, RAG, MCP/resource access, memory, or deterministic code [ts=5298s]. The instructor emphasizes LLM traces as essential for debugging because they expose which prompts and tools were called when failures happen [ts=5427s]. The eval taxonomy combines component-based and end-to-end views with objective/subjective and quantitative/qualitative measurements [ts=5475s].

key_points.text: A practical agent project should start by decomposing the human task and identifying difficult or fuzzy steps.
The shipping-address workflow includes extraction, customer record retrieval, policy check, response drafting, and email sending.
Workflow design maps each decomposed step to LLM, RAG, tool, MCP/resource access, memory, or deterministic logic.
LLM extraction is likely enough for identifying the intent, order number, and new address.
Database lookup and address update require a tool or resource/MCP access rather than just text generation.
LLM traces are foundational for debugging because they show the chain of prompts and where bugs occur.
Component-based evals inspect each step separately, while end-to-end evals measure overall user experience.
Objective issues can be programmatically checked; subjective ones may need human ratings or LLM-as-judge rubrics.
Quantitative evals include success rates and latency; qualitative evals inspect hallucinations, tone mismatches, and user confusion.

kp_catalog.name: Customer support task decomposition
kp_catalog.description: Breaking a support-agent workflow into information extraction, record lookup, policy check, response drafting, email sending, and selecting the right technology for each step.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The customer-support case study is the concrete worked example used to teach task decomposition and workflow mapping [ts=5236s].

kp_catalog.name: LLM traces for debugging
kp_catalog.description: Recorded traces of prompts, tool calls, and intermediate outputs that make it possible to locate failures inside an LLM workflow.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor explicitly calls traces a basic part of an AI startup stack and recommends asking about them during interviews [ts=5427s].

kp_catalog.name: Agent eval taxonomy
kp_catalog.description: Evaluation dimensions for LLM agents: objective versus subjective, component-based versus end-to-end, and quantitative versus qualitative.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Agent evaluation is important for implementation quality, but supports the agentic workflow gateway.
